## Practical 6: Introduction

The first part of this practical aims to build a bioinformatics web server that predicts **m6A site probabilities and statuses** from new input features. The second part requires you to integrate the Shiny web server code as an **ML prediction module** into the bioinformatics database you built in the last practical.

> **Note:** This practical is **assessed** and accounts for **10%** of the final course mark.  
> The submission deadline is **November 4 (next Tuesday) at 23:59**.  
> The mark will be awarded equally between the database (from Practical 5) and the web server (from this practical); in other words, each part contributes **50%** of your submission mark.  
> Marks will be based on how complete and functional your website is for each part. Missing critical components, having functional or display errors, or lacking clarity in documentation will result in mark deductions.

The **only accepted submission format** is a single URL hosted on [shinyapps.io](https://www.shinyapps.io/).  
To do this:

1. Create an account on [shinyapps.io](https://www.shinyapps.io/).  
2. Store your Shiny code in an R file named **`app.R`**.  
3. Deploy your app using `rsconnect::deployApp("app.R")` or by clicking the **Publish** button in RStudio IDE.

After successfully sharing your app, copy your URL and submit it through the **LMO submission box** (in questionnaire form).

## Task 1: Build a web server that supports the prediction of m6A sites from input features (50%)

### Step 1: Prepare the ML classification model to predict m6A site probabilities and statuses from new data

Train a Random Forest model using the `RandomForest` R package with the **entire dataset** `../../data/m6A_imbalanced.csv`.  
Use the following input features:  
`gc_content`, `RNA_type`, `RNA_region`, `exon_length`, `distance_to_junction`, `evolutionary_conservation`, and `DNA_5mer`.

Convert the DNA sequences in `DNA_5mer` into **one-hot encoding** before training the model, as demonstrated in previous practicals.  
Set the random seed using `set.seed(123)` to ensure reproducibility.

After training the model, save the fitted model object (returned by `RandomForest()`) into a variable named `rf_fit`.  
Export `rf_fit` to your hard disk as an RDS file named **`rf_fit.rds`** using `saveRDS()`.

> **Note:**  
> The code for data input and DNA encoding has been provided.  
> <mark>In this practical, we will **strictly specify the factor levels and their order** for all categorical features, including `RNA_type`, `RNA_region`, and `nt_pos1–5`.</mark>  
> <mark>This step is crucial for maintaining prediction reliability when users query only a few data points inputs.</mark>  
> <mark>提前将分类变量设定为Factor, 防止用户输入时某些分类变量类别不全, 引起潜在问题</mark>

```{r, eval=TRUE}
#Load input data
data_df <- read.csv("../../data/m6A_imbalanced.csv")

#Define function for DNA sequence encoding
dna_encoding <- function(dna_strings){
nn <- nchar( dna_strings[1] )
seq_m <- matrix( unlist( strsplit(dna_strings, "") ), ncol = nn, byrow = TRUE)
colnames(seq_m) <- paste0("nt_pos", 1:nn)
seq_df <- as.data.frame(seq_m)
seq_df[] <- lapply(seq_df, factor, levels = c("A", "T", "C", "G"))
return(seq_df)
}

# Encode DNA sequence and set factor levels for categorical variables
data_df <- cbind(data_df, dna_encoding(data_df$DNA_5mer))
data_df$m6A_status <- factor(data_df$m6A_status, levels = c("Negative", "Positive"))
data_df$RNA_type <- factor(data_df$RNA_type, levels = c("mRNA", "lincRNA", "lncRNA", "pseudogene"))
data_df$RNA_region <- factor(data_df$RNA_region, levels = c("CDS", "intron", "3'UTR", "5'UTR"))

# Fill the code under `___`
# 1. fit random forest model (identical "nt_pos3" is excluded to avoid multicollinearity)
rf_fit <- randomForest(data = data_df, m6A_status ~ gc_content + RNA_type + RNA_region  + exon_length + distance_to_junction + evolutionary_conservation + nt_pos1 + nt_pos2 + nt_pos4 + nt_pos5)

# 2. check model
rf_fit

# 3. save fitted model as an RDS file
saveRDS(rf_fit, file = "rf_fit.rds")
```

### Step 2: Prepare the exemplar data for ML prediction input

Randomly sample **100 rows** from `../../data/m6A_imbalanced.csv` using `sample.int()`, and keep only the input feature columns:  
`gc_content`, `RNA_type`, `RNA_region`, `exon_length`, `distance_to_junction`, `evolutionary_conservation`, and `DNA_5mer`.  
Name this sampled subset `example_data`.

Save the subsetted data frame as a new CSV file named **`m6A_input_example.csv`**.  
When exporting the exemplar data with `write.csv()`, set the argument `row.names = FALSE`.

```{r, eval=TRUE}
# Fill your code at the `___`
# 1. sample 100 rows
sample_row_idx <- sample.int(nrow(data_df), size = 100, replace = FALSE)

# 2. generate subset with specified columns
keep_cols <- c("gc_content", "RNA_type", "RNA_region", "exon_length", "distance_to_junction", "evolutionary_conservation", "DNA_5mer")
example_data <- data_df[sample_row_idx, keep_cols]

# export as .csv
write.csv(example_data, file = "m6A_input_example.csv", row.names = FALSE)

head(example_data)
```

### Step 3: Prepare an R function that can make predictions from an input feature data frame

Now we will create an R function named `prediction_multiple()` to make predictions from a data frame of input features.  
We do this so that the Shiny server can call one clean function and run smoothly later.

You will complete the function template below. The function takes three arguments: `ml_fit`, `feature_df`, and `positive_threshold`.

- `ml_fit`: the fitted Random Forest model object (e.g. `rf_fit`).
- `feature_df`: a data frame that must contain the seven input features used by the model.
- `positive_threshold`: a numeric value between 0 and 1 that defines the decision threshold for the positive class.

Your task is to complete the function so that:

1. It performs prediction using the provided model.

2. It returns the original `feature_df`, augmented with two new columns:  

   - `predicted_m6A_prob`: the predicted positive-class probability for each row.  
   - `predicted_m6A_status`: either `"Positive"` or `"Negative"` for each row, depending on whether the predicted probability is greater than the specified threshold.

In other words, the output should be the input `feature_df` plus these two additional columns.

> <mark>Note: At the beginning of the function, you must set the factor level order of all categorical variables to match the levels used during model training. This is critical for consistent and reliable predictions.</mark>

```{r, eval=TRUE}
prediction_multiple <- function(ml_fit, feature_df, positive_threshold = 0.5){
  stopifnot(all(c("gc_content", "RNA_type", "RNA_region", "exon_length", "distance_to_junction", "evolutionary_conservation", "DNA_5mer") %in% colnames(feature_df))) #Check errors if incorrect column names of input data.frame

  # Complete this function by writing code at the `___`
  # 1. process input data
  feature_df <- cbind(feature_df, dna_encoding(feature_df$DNA_5mer))
  feature_df$RNA_type <- factor(feature_df$RNA_type, levels = c("mRNA", "lincRNA", "lncRNA", "pseudogene"))
  feature_df$RNA_region <- factor(feature_df$RNA_region, levels = c("CDS", "intron", "3'UTR", "5'UTR"))

  # 2. predict and classify
  prob <- predict(ml_fit, feature_df, type = "prob")
  prob_binary <- ifelse(prob[, 2] <= positive_threshold, "Negative", "Positive")

  # 3. add rows for output
  feature_df$predicted_m6A_prob <- prob[, 2] # predicted positive-class probability
  feature_df$predicted_m6A_status <- prob_binary # either "Positive" or "Negative"
  feature_df$predicted_m6A_status <- factor(feature_df$predicted_m6A_status, levels = c("Negative", "Positive"))

  # 4. delete expanded one-hot DNA-5mer columns
  feature_df <- subset(feature_df, select = -c(nt_pos1, nt_pos2, nt_pos3, nt_pos4, nt_pos5))

  return(feature_df) #return a data.frame with supplied columns of predicted m6A prob and predicted m6A status
}

head(prediction_multiple(rf_fit, example_data, positive_threshold = 0.5))
```

### Step 4: Prepare an R function that can make a prediction from a single data point

Next, we will create another function named `prediction_single()` that takes the input features of a single data point and generates a prediction for that data point.

This function uses the same arguments `ml_fit` and `positive_threshold` as in `prediction_multiple()`, but instead of taking a full data frame, it will take seven additional arguments corresponding to the input feature values of the model.  
The goal is to allow the server to predict from one manually entered set of feature values.

The key requirement is the same as before:  
you must convert all categorical input values to factors, and you must set their factor levels to match those used during model training.

After formatting the inputs, the function should:

1. Construct a single-row data frame using the provided feature values.
2. Call `prediction_multiple()` internally on that one-row data frame.
3. Extract the prediction results.

The returned object from `prediction_single()` should be a **named vector of length 2**, containing:

- the predicted m6A probability, and  
- the predicted m6A status.

The names of the vector should be set to:  
`c("predicted_m6A_prob", "predicted_m6A_status")`.

```{r, eval=TRUE}
prediction_single <- function(ml_fit, gc_content, RNA_type, RNA_region, exon_length, distance_to_junction, evolutionary_conservation, DNA_5mer, positive_threshold = 0.5){

  # Complete this function by writing code at the `___`
  # 1. construct single-row data frame
  single_row_df <- data.frame(
    gc_content = as.numeric(gc_content),
    RNA_type = RNA_type,
    RNA_region = RNA_region,
    exon_length = as.numeric(exon_length),
    distance_to_junction = as.numeric(distance_to_junction),
    evolutionary_conservation = as.numeric(evolutionary_conservation),
    DNA_5mer = toupper(trimws(DNA_5mer))
  )
  
  # 2. evoke prediction_multiple() (factor convertion will be conducted automatically here)
  results_full <- prediction_multiple(ml_fit, single_row_df, positive_threshold)
  
  # 3. extract prediction results
  returned_vector <- c(results_full[1, "predicted_m6A_prob"], as.character(results_full[1, "predicted_m6A_status"]))
  names(returned_vector) <- c("predicted_m6A_prob", "predicted_m6A_status")
  
  return(returned_vector) #return a named vector with values for predicted m6A prob and predicted m6A status
}

prediction_single(rf_fit, gc_content = 0.5, 
                          RNA_type = "mRNA", 
                          RNA_region = "CDS", 
                          exon_length = 10, 
                          distance_to_junction = 8, 
                          evolutionary_conservation = 0.5, 
                          DNA_5mer = "GGACA", 
                          positive_threshold = 0.5)
```

### Step 5: Design Shiny UI and server code to build a bioinformatics web server that can predict m6A sites

Next, you will create a Shiny web page using `dashboardPage()` from the `shinydashboard` package.

This page should allow the user to:

1. Upload a CSV file containing input features.
2. View the uploaded table.
3. Run m6A prediction on the table.
4. Download the prediction results.

#### Required behavior

- The user uploads a CSV file.  
  On the server side, you should read the file into a data frame and display it using `renderDT()` from the `DT` package.

- The UI must include a **"Predict"** button.  
  When the user clicks this button, the server should run the `prediction_multiple()` function (from Step 3) on the uploaded data frame.  
  The function will return a new data frame that contains all original feature columns plus two additional columns:
  - `predicted_m6A_prob`
  - `predicted_m6A_status`

  These correspond to the predicted m6A probability and the predicted m6A status for each row.

- After prediction, the displayed table should update to show this augmented data frame (i.e. the new version replaces the old one in the UI).

- The UI must also include a **"Download"** button.  
  Clicking it should download the full augmented data frame (with predictions) as a CSV file named `predicted.csv`.

#### Example data button

Include an additional button called **"Example data"**.  
When clicked, it should automatically load the example data from `m6A_input_example.csv` (created in Step 2) and display it in the table.  
This acts as a demo input for users who do not have their own CSV ready.

#### Decision threshold control

Add a slider bar using `sliderInput()` to control the decision threshold passed to the `positive_threshold` argument in `prediction_multiple()`.  
Users should be able to choose the probability cutoff that defines `"Positive"` vs `"Negative"`.

- The default value of the slider should be `0.5`.  
- The range of the slider should be from `0` to `1`.

Changing this slider should trigger a reactive update of the predictions in the displayed `DT` table.

#### Page layout

A single menu page called **"m6A Prediction Multiple"** is sufficient for this functionality.

Because the table will have many columns and many rows, configure the data table with  
`options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 15)`  
inside `renderDT()` to enable horizontal scrolling and to show more rows per page.

Arrange the UI so that:

- The input / control panel (file upload, example data button, threshold slider, Predict button, Download button) is vertically stacked **above** the table output panel.
- Each section has a short header to guide the user step by step. For example:
  - **Step 1. Upload an input feature CSV file**
  - **Step 2. Select a decision threshold for the positive class probability**
  - **Step 3. Click `Predict` to run inference**

### Step 6: Add a manual input page to the web server for single-observation prediction

Next, building on the webpage you created above, add one additional menu page called **"m6A Prediction Single"**.  
This page allows users to manually enter the feature values for a single observation.  
The output will be two values: the predicted m6A probability and the predicted m6A status.  
This helps users understand the model’s behavior in a more direct and intuitive way.

Users will manually specify the values of the following features:

- `RNA_type`: provided by a `selectInput()`.  
  Allowed values: `"mRNA"`, `"lincRNA"`, `"lncRNA"`, `"pseudogene"`.  
  Default value: `"mRNA"`.

- `RNA_region`: provided by a `selectInput()`.  
  Allowed values: `"CDS"`, `"intron"`, `"3'UTR"`, `"5'UTR"`.  
  Default value: `"CDS"`.

- `gc_content`: provided by a `sliderInput()`.  
  Range: `0` to `1`.  
  Default: `0.5`.

- `exon_length`: provided by a `sliderInput()`.  
  Range: `0` to `15`.  
  Default: `10`.

- `distance_to_junction`: provided by a `sliderInput()`.  
  Range: `0` to `15`.  
  Default: `8`.

- `evolutionary_conservation`: provided by a `sliderInput()`.  
  Range: `0` to `1`.  
  Default: `0.5`.

- `DNA_5mer`: provided by a `textInput()`.  
  The input must be a DNA string of length 5.  
  Only the characters `"A"`, `"T"`, `"C"`, and `"G"` are allowed.  
  Default: `"GGACA"`.

The prediction for a single instance will be generated using the `prediction_single()` function.  
This function returns a named vector with two values:

- predicted m6A probability  
- predicted m6A status  

These values should be displayed to the user in a visually clear way (for example, in a value box or info box).

The prediction results must update **reactively**:  
any change in the input values above should immediately trigger a new prediction.  
No submit button is required on this page.

For layout:

- Arrange the input panel horizontally or in a vertical box on the **left side**.
- Display the prediction output (probability + status) on the **right side** in a dedicated results panel.
- Include brief usage instructions, such as:
  - “Set the feature values below.”  
  - “The model will automatically predict whether this site is m6A (‘Positive’ or ‘Negative’).”  
  - “The probability score reflects model confidence.”

### Website publication

A step-by-step guide to publishing your final app product:

1. Register an account with your email at [shinyapps.io](https://www.shinyapps.io/).  
   Click **Sign Up**, enter your information, and log in.

2. Create a new R script named **`app.R`**.  
   Copy and paste the entire code of your app into this file and save it.  
   The code in `app.R` must contain a **complete single app**, starting from `library(...)`, including data loading, function definitions, `ui`, `server`, and ending with a call to `shinyApp(ui, server)`.
   
3. Copy your shinyapps.io token from this page:  
   [https://www.shinyapps.io/admin/#/tokens](https://www.shinyapps.io/admin/#/tokens)  
   Select **Show** → **Copy to Clipboard** → press **Ctrl + C** and **Enter**.

4. Open the `app.R` file in **RStudio IDE**.  

   For R studio server:
    Click the **Publish** button → select **Publish all documents in the directory** → **Next** → choose **shinyapps.io** → paste your token code (copied from Step 3) into the box → **Connect Account**.

   For R studio desktop:
   Click the **Publish** button → select **Posit Connect** → **Publish Document with Source Code** → **Next** → choose **shinyapps.io** → **Connect** → paste your token code (copied from Step 3) into the box → **Connect**.
   
5. Select all necessary files, including:  
   - `app.R`  
   - `rf_fit.rds`  
   - `m6A_input_example.csv`  
   - `../../data/m6A_imbalanced.csv`  

   Enter your project Title as **`P6[Your Student ID]`**, then click **Publish**.  
   Wait until the browser automatically opens and displays your deployed website.  
   Copy the URL and submit it on **LMO**.

Once deployed, your URL can be accessed by anyone with an internet connection.  
You can test it by opening the link in your phone’s browser.

### Final recommendation

<mark>
A well-designed image illustrating the biological entities or concepts in your database and server can be a strong visual highlight for your bioinformatics webpage.
</mark>

<mark>
Nowadays, you can easily create such an image by prompting an AI image generator with detailed information about your project’s background and purpose.
</mark>

<mark>
It is highly recommended that everyone developing their website for the final Capstone project include an **illustrative image** on the **home page** of their website. Successfully adding an image to this submission will also help you secure a perfect score.
</mark>

<mark>
This visual element helps communicate the **biological purpose** and **key service design** of your project more effectively.
</mark>

<mark>
You can display an image in your Shiny app using `imageOutput()` in the UI and `renderImage()` in the server.  
Make sure to place your image file in the same directory as your `app.R` file, and specify its path correctly within `renderImage()`.
</mark>
